extracted.intended_audience: instructors, TAs, and students involved in undergraduate applied mathematics courses (esp. those teaching or supervising communication-intensive assignments)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and rubrics for designing, assigning, grading, and giving feedback on undergraduate applied-mathematics writing and presentations, plus TA training and supervision for consistent assessment. Focuses on short writing tasks, algorithm descriptions, audience-targeted explanations, linear-program analyses, peer critique, and (historically) term papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove a given statement (short writing assignment, 1-2 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: Prove a given statement. (1-2 pages). Many students have not written proofs before, and proof-writing is an important focus of the class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication objectives: proof writing, precision, rigor, guiding text. Handout: formatting a proof and using guiding text. The short-writing rubric is used for grading these assignments (same rubric for draft and revision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe an algorithm and calculate its running time (2-3 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: Describe an algorithm and calculate its running time. (2-3 pages). The algorithm is complex enough that students must introduce and explain sub-algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication objectives: structure; defining terms; context vs. detail. Notes enumerate structural challenges students face (present as sequence vs. high-level-first; when to present running-time calculations; whether to present sub-algorithms before/after; when to state definitions). A handout is provided: 'Handout re: explaining algorithms.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain a topic to two different audiences (2-3 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: Explain a topic in discrete applied mathematics to two different audiences. (2-3 pages). Students choose two contexts/questions from several related contexts and must adjust explanations accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication objectives: rhetorical analysis of context (including audience knowledge and purpose), designing communication appropriately given the context (including level of detail). Option to write a dialogue when an oral response is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze a linear program and its dual (5 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: Analyze a linear program and its dual. (5 pages). Students choose from several suggested linear programs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication objectives: structure, focus, cohesion, and smaller-scale issues as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Term paper (10+ pages) — historical assignment
rubrics_metrics.description: Previously used assignment: Term paper on a topic of the student's choice. (10+ pages). Guidance for choosing a term paper topic was provided; this assignment was later suspended in large offering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communication objectives: structure, focus, cohesion, and smaller-scale issues as needed. Instructor observations note term paper value is higher in smaller classes where individual topic guidance is feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer critique (1-2 pages)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignment: Peer critique. (1-2 pages). Conducted online rather than face-to-face due to scheduling; students reported online critique of shorter writing assignments isn’t very helpful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Handout: Peer review guidance plus rubric. Peer-critique assignment has been used historically but may be less effective online for short pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubric for short writing assignments (Spring 1010)
rubrics_metrics.description: A short-writing rubric used for the sake of simplicity and consistency; used for both first-draft and revision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rubric is the primary grading instrument for short assignments and is used consistently across graders; TAs are trained to use it and norm on it. (File referenced: 'Rubric for short writing').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for grading term-paper drafts (Spring 2009)
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidance used when draft receives a grade based on effort/completeness and an advisory grade for writing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students were assigned a draft grade based on effort/completeness and an advisory writing grade that could be revised after revision. (File referenced: 'Guidance for grading the term paper draft').

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for assigning grades to drafts and revisions when draft is graded for effort
rubrics_metrics.description: A rubric/guidance exists for assigning grades to drafts and revisions when the draft receives a grade based only on effort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This guidance clarifies how to convert effort/completeness grades and advisory writing grades into final assessments after revision. (Note: this specific rubric was noted as not currently used.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for identifying and responding to suspected plagiarism
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural guidance for how to identify and respond to suspected plagiarism in student writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course provides a specific guidance document to TAs on identifying and responding to suspected plagiarism (file referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: TA training: using a single rubric and team norming
rubrics_metrics.description: TAs are trained to comment on writing by instructors and a WAC lecturer; training emphasizes using a single rubric throughout the term and conducting norming sessions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shortly after first papers arrive, the entire team meets to discuss how to use the rubric. For the first several assignments, the team meets after grading to ensure consistent grading: TAs bring grades and reasons, identify best/worst papers; those papers are circulated; middle-boundary papers circulated if needed. Meetings typically require an hour/week and include discussion of important writing characteristics and how to write effective comments. Once consistency is achieved, weekly meetings may be suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: TA training: redundancy with WAC lecturer and shared comments
rubrics_metrics.description: For each assignment, some papers graded by each TA are also commented on by the WAC lecturer to train TAs and allow lecturer assessment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All WAC-lecturer comments are made available to all TAs so they can learn from modeled comments and the lecturer can assess and guide TA commenting practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading practice: anchor grading by instructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructor grades three papers (one strong, one weak, one average) quickly after assignment due; these grades serve as anchors for other graders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Throughout term, graders are reminded to give honest praise in addition to constructive feedback; graders are encouraged to recognize improvement as the term progresses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading principle: praise plus constructive feedback & recognize improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: When commenting and grading, give honest praise as well as constructive feedback and be attentive to student improvement over the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is emphasized during TA training and grading meetings to support student learning and encourage continued progress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance for grading second-language learners
rubrics_metrics.description: Advice for commenting and grading work by students for whom English is a second language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be realistic about expectations; developing fluency takes years. Comment on grammatical issues (articles, prepositions, numbers) only once and then ignore them to avoid overwhelming the student. Optionally underline grammatical issues to help the student self-identify and correct. Suggest asking a friend to help or using a grammar checker (with caveats). Comment and grade primarily on issues that affect clarity (word choice, guiding text, structure). Note cultural structural styles and point out commonly used structures in American academic mathematics writing. For recurring grammar/word-choice mistakes, note once and suggest adding them to an 'editing checklist' or vocabulary list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective: proof-writing quality (precision, rigor, guiding text)
rubrics_metrics.description: Key evaluative focus for proof-writing assignments: students must demonstrate proof-writing ability with attention to precision, mathematical rigor, and use of guiding text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting materials include a handout on formatting a proof and using guiding text; rubrics evaluate clarity of argument, level of detail, and the presence of guiding sentences that orient the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective: structure, defining terms, context vs detail (algorithm descriptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative foci for algorithm-description tasks include structural organization, clear definition of terms, and appropriate choices about context and level-of-detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should decide whether to present a sequence of steps or high-level approach first, when to present running-time analysis, and how to order sub-algorithms and definitions for maximal clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective: rhetorical analysis and audience adaptation
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must analyze rhetorical context (audience knowledge and purpose) and design communication appropriate to that context, including adjusting level of detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments may require producing two versions for different audiences; option to craft dialogue for oral contexts; evaluate appropriateness of tone, vocabulary, and explanatory depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Communication objective: structure, focus, cohesion (longer assignments)
rubrics_metrics.description: For longer pieces (linear-program analyses, term papers), evaluate structure, focus, cohesion, and finer-scale issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how well the document is organized, whether it stays focused on the main goals, and whether transitions and connections support reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering information and connectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: order information so content flows logically and guide the audience through the content; avoid excessive connectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The course addresses 'Information Order and Connectivity' and cautions against excessive connectivity (too many linking statements) while emphasizing the need to structure content to guide the reader effectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balancing conceptual vs. formal exposition; precision and rigor
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: balance conceptual explanation with formal mathematical detail, while maintaining precision and rigor appropriate to audience and purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should be evaluated on their ability to present intuition and conceptual understanding alongside formal definitions and proofs, selecting the right balance for their intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proof structure and proof elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: attention to proof structure and proof elegance as part of evaluating mathematical exposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage strategies for proof-writing, recognize different proof types, and value elegance where appropriate (conciseness, clarity, insightful steps) while not sacrificing rigor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience awareness (general principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principle: awareness of the audience should inform level of explanation, notation choices, and rhetorical decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Included as a major topic area: 'Audience Awareness'—used across assignments and presentations to evaluate appropriateness of language, examples, and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using sources, visuals, wording/punctuation, and notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles and practical criteria for using external sources, designing visuals, choosing wording and punctuation, and selecting notation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Course resources include handouts on 'Using sources', 'Using visuals', 'Wording and punctuation', and 'Notation' (and LaTeX guidance). Grading should consider proper attribution, clarity of figures, readable notation, and correct/clear punctuation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment: objective grading of subjective communication
rubrics_metrics.description: Question addressed in resources: How can one objectively grade something as subjective as communication?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The site offers materials on feedback and assessment for writing, providing rubrics and structured criteria to reduce subjectivity (consistent rubric use, norming, anchors, focus on clarity/structure/precision).
